title: Every Fraction of a Degree Counts for the Planet
summary:
Countries are gathered in Turkey for COP31, the climate talks, to tackle a goal that is slipping away. Ten years ago, nations agreed to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Now, scientists say that goal is out of reach.

The planet is nearly 1.5 degrees warmer than it was before the Industrial Revolution. Heat-trapping emissions from burning fossil fuels are still rising, and most countries are not on track to meet their climate promises to switch to cleaner energy.

A United Nations study says the best case now is 1.7 or 1.8 degrees of warming. If emissions stay on their current path, the world could be 2.8 degrees hotter by the end of the century.

The difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees may sound tiny, but research shows it changes everything. "The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, a climate professor at the University of Exeter. "Every fraction of a degree that we avoid is really able to do a huge amount of limiting harm."

Coral reefs show why. Corals build the framework that supports vast numbers of other species. But corals are very sensitive to heat. Long marine heat waves turn them white, a process called bleaching, which can eventually kill them. There have been four global bleaching events since the late 1990s, and scientists say a fifth may now be unfolding.

Researchers found that before the 2023 to 2025 bleaching event, 44 percent of coral species were at risk of extinction. Beyond 2 degrees of warming, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found, 99 percent of corals would be lost.

Countries are focusing on electrification: cars and homes running on electricity instead of fossil fuels, since much of the world's electricity now comes from solar and wind.
why_it_matters: Every fraction of a degree of warming decides how much of the natural world survives, from coral reefs to the weather children will grow up with, so the choices made at COP31 shape the planet they will inherit.

background_read: At climate talks like COP31, countries from around the world meet to agree on how to limit global warming and cut the heat-trapping gases released when fossil fuels are burned.
The goal they set was to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above the temperatures before the Industrial Revolution, when factories and machines began burning large amounts of coal, oil, and gas.

Even small amounts of extra warming matter because hotter oceans stress coral reefs, which provide homes and shelter for many other sea creatures, and long heat waves can turn corals white and kill them.
One way countries are trying to cut emissions is electrification, which means powering cars and homes with electricity, much of which now comes from cleaner sources like solar and wind.
